summary: Subsystem quantum error correction enables Heisenberg-limit metrology with substantially reduced overhead compared to standard QEC approaches, requiring at most a single ancilla qubit and syndrome-free recovery procedures. The framework extends to time-dependent signals through Floquet codes, which protect periodic metrological evolution by dynamically encoding information in a logical subsystem while allowing noise to be absorbed into gauge degrees of freedom.
motivation: Existing QEC-assisted metrology requires multiple noiseless ancillae and complex mid-circuit syndrome measurements with feedback, creating significant experimental barriers to reaching the Heisenberg limit in realistic systems.
method: The authors derive conditions under which subsystem stabilizer codes achieve the Heisenberg limit (Theorem 1), then prove that broad noise classes admit syndrome-free protocols with zero or one noiseless ancilla (Theorem 2). They extend this to dynamical error correction using ladder codes, where time-varying signals synchronize with periodically rotating check measurements over four rounds to maintain logical coherence.
result: For correctable Pauli noise satisfying the HNKS condition $H \notin \mathrm{Span}\{\langle E_1, \ldots, E_r \rangle\}$, syndrome-free subsystem codes achieve $F_Q(\rho_\theta^{(N)}) \propto N^2$ with only gauge reset applied after each query, and no ancilla is required when the noise algebra occupies fewer than $n$ qubits or when a commuting component of $H$ exists outside the noise span.
